title: RESOLUTION TO SUPPORT THE YOUTH JUSTICE INNOVATION FUND
resolution_text_full:
RESOLUTION TO SUPPORT THE YOUTH JUSTICE INNOVATION FUND
(S.642/A.10264) - COMMUNITY BOARD 10
Resolution in Support of the Youth Justice Innovation Fund (S.642/A.10264) sponsored by
Senator Cordell Cleare and Assemblymember Gabriella Romero to invest $50 million from the
Raise the Age appropriation into the Youth Justice Innovation Fund.
WHEREAS, investment in youth and young adults is a matter of public safety and community
health; and
WHEREAS, the Youth Justice Innovation Fund (S.642/A.10264) would establish a fund,
managed by the Department of Criminal Justice Services, that would expedite funding to
community-based organizations that work directly with young people and young adults ages
12-25 in supporting prevention, alternatives to incarceration, and reentry care.
WHEREAS, New York passed Raise the Age legislation in 2017 that raised the age of criminal
prosecution of children from 16 to 18 years of age, and since then has appropriated $1.71 billion
to fund the law’s implementation and youth programming that supports young people and
promotes public safety; and
WHEREAS, less than half of those appropriated funds have been dispersed for use; and
WHEREAS, the slow dispersal of appropriated funds has prevented the Raise the Age funding
statute from living up to its promise of ensuring all eligible youth receive appropriate
programmatic services; and
WHEREAS, the FY2027 budget appropriates $250 million to fund much-needed youth
programming; and
WHEREAS, the Youth Justice Innovation Fund would make $50 million of the $250 million
appropriation directly available to community-based organizations; and
WHEREAS, the $50 million is already earmarked for Raise the Age programming, and the
Youth Justice Innovation Fund would facilitate its administration directly to community-based
programs; and
WHEREAS, the community-based organizations that would receive Youth Justice Innovation
Fund support follow successful, evidence-based models to improve youth outcomes, such as
exalt, CASES, SNUG Albany, and the Erie County Restorative Justice Coalition, among others;
and
WHEREAS, programs operating in New York City are not eligible to receive Raise the Age
funding, despite New York City youth comprising approximately 50% of the youth involved in
the justice system statewide, the Youth Justice Innovation Fund would be available statewide;
and
WHEREAS, the Raise the Age funding only supports programming for 16-and 17-year-olds, the
Youth Justice Innovation Fund would support programming for young people ages 12-25,
allowing more New Yorkers and their communities to benefit from evidence-based
programming;
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Manhattan Community Board Ten endorses enactment
of the Youth Justice Innovation Fund for the purposes of promoting community safety, youth
investment, and healthy, well-resourced communities.

title: RESOLUTION REQUESTING A FORMAL REVIEW OF COMMUNITY BOARD 10
resolution_text_full:
RESOLUTION REQUESTING A FORMAL REVIEW OF COMMUNITY BOARD 10
BOUNDARIES AND ESTABLISHING INTER-BOARD COLLABORATION REGARDING
CENTRAL HARLEM PARKS
WHEREAS, pursuant to New York City Charter § 2800, Community Boards are charged with
providing meaningful community input on land use, service delivery, capital budgeting, and the
general welfare of their districts; and
WHEREAS, the Manhattan Borough President, under NYC Charter § 2800(d), holds oversight
authority to review and recommend changes to community board boundaries in consultation with
the Department of City Planning and other stakeholders; and
WHEREAS, the current boundaries of Manhattan Community District 10 do not fully encompass
the following key public parklands that directly serve the Harlem community:
● Marcus Garvey Park
● Harlem River Park
● Morningside Park
● St. Nicholas Park
● Central Park North
WHEREAS, these parks are vital recreational, cultural, historical, and environmental assets for
Central Harlem residents, and the present boundaries create fragmented administrative oversight,
complicating advocacy for capital resources, maintenance, and programming; and
WHEREAS, effective governance of these shared parks requires inter-district cooperation and,
where appropriate, reconsideration of boundary lines to reflect geographic, cultural, and practical
realities of community use;
NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED THAT:
1. Manhattan Community Board 10 formally requests that the Manhattan Borough President,
pursuant to NYC Charter § 2800(d), initiate a comprehensive review of Community District
10’s boundaries, specifically concerning Marcus Garvey Park, Harlem River Park,
Morningside Park, and St. Nicholas Park.
2. Manhattan Community Board 10 authorizes its Parks and Recreation Committee Chair to
engage Community Boards 9 and 11 in creating a formal inter-board working group for joint
planning, advocacy, and oversight of these shared parks.
3. Manhattan Community Board 10 commits to full participation in any assessment,
consultation, or public hearing process convened by the Manhattan Borough President,
Department of City Planning, or other relevant city agencies.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED THAT: This resolution shall be transmitted to the Manhattan
Borough President, Department of City Planning, Department of Parks and Recreation, Community
Boards 9 and 11, and the appropriate City Council Members. Manhattan Community Board 10 during
the specially held June Board meeting before the board breaks for the summer, held on June 25, 2025 voted
unanimously to issue this resolution with 30 Yes, 0 No, 0 Excused 0 Abstentions.
Adopted this 25th day of June, 2025

title: Resolution to Safeguard Essential Services and Dignified
resolution_text_full:
Resolution to Safeguard Essential Services and Dignified
Aging for Older Adults in Manhattan Community Board 10
WHEREAS The United States Executive branch under the administration of President Donald J. Trump is
implementing a wide array of legislative changes that will impact the senior population of Manhattan CB 10
and seniors throughout the nation; and
[1]
WHEREAS 12.2% percent of the 138,953 Central Harlem population is 65+ ; and
WHEREAS The U.S. is witnessing an unprecedented wave of Baby Boomers (those born between 1946 and
1964) retirements, with approximately 10,000 Boomers turning 65 each day. Around 3.2 million and 3.5
million people retired in 2022 and 2023 respectively, with 3.6 million expected by 2024. By 2030, the entire
Boomer generation – comprising around 73 million people – will have reached retirement age, significantly
reshaping the U.S. workforce. Between 2024 and 2030, 30.4 million baby boomers will turn 65. This
demographic shift is expected to decrease the labor force participation rate from 62% in 2023 to roughly 58%
by 2030. While fewer job seekers will push the unemployment rate down, potentially below 3%, the resulting
labor shortages will present wage pressures and skill mismatch challenges for key industries like healthcare,
[2]
education, and manufacturing ; and
WHEREAS Cuts to Medicare/Medicaid or shifts in eligibility standards could preclude seniors from
qualifying for Medicaid services. The Medicaid/Medicare services are helping seniors to maintain such
quality-of-life issues as: (1) living in the community/in their own homes and aging in place, (2) getting
preventative healthcare services, (3) seeing their medical provider regularly, (4) receiving life-sustaining
medications, and (5) staying out of the hospital; and
WHEREAS The current administration has made major cuts to federal programs, including the Social
Security Administration (SSA), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) (including Medicare and
Medicaid) and Veterans Administration (VA); and
WHEREAS The current administration, acting with Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), has
fired over 25,000 federal workers, including at the SSA, HHS and VA; and
WHEREAS Retirees rely on critical services provided by the SSA, HHS and VA; and
WHEREAS Lower staffing levels are already disrupting the administration of these agencies and their ability
to serve our communities; and
WHEREAS Labor unions have long struggled against arbitrary cuts and dismissals in our workplaces; and
WHEREAS Many supportive medical devices and supplies that seniors depend upon are produced abroad
and will be impacted by the Trump tariff activities through increased costs and decreased access; and
WHEREAS Since January, 2025 and 12 weeks into the year, Donald J. Trump has signed 129 Executive
[3]
orders (from EO 14147 through EO 14275) ; and
WHEREAS Aging should be experienced with dignity, regardless of financial circumstances—free from the
worry, harm, and injustice caused by lack of health care, food insecurity, or a safe place to sleep. Our seniors
should all be able to access the resources, services, and programs needed to thrive as they grow older, no
matter their financial circumstances, where they come from, their race, gender, gender identity, sexual
[4]
orientation, ability, or language ; and
WHEREAS Older adults anchor our families and communities and connect our families through the
generations. But after working all their lives, nearly half of our nation’s older adults living alone struggle to
pay for food, rent, and medical care, and rely on Social Security, SSI, Medicare and Medicaid to survive; and
WHEREAS The Medicare and Medicaid programs are crucial for older adults, people with disabilities, and
their families. 67 million people are enrolled in Medicare, with 12.5 million enrolled in both Medicare and
Medicaid. We must continue to ensure everyone can access the comprehensive, high quality, affordable health
and long-term care needed to age in dignity. If lawmakers seek to reduce funding for programs, restrict
eligibility for Medicare and Medicaid or limit the type or scope of services available, the Community will
need to work together to stop them; and
WHEREAS Access to long-term care should be strengthened and extended with respect to Medicare and
Medicaid so older adults can age in their homes and communities and ensure that nursing facilities provide
high quality care and dignity for residents. Lawmakers who seek to make changes that result in reduced
access to home care or endanger nursing facility residents must be opposed; and
WHEREAS Social Security and Supplemental Security Income (SSI) are the backbone of economic security
for older adults, lifting over 16.5 million older adults out of poverty. With nearly five million older Americans
living on less than $1,000 a month, these programs are crucial. Work should be continued to improve these
vital programs and make benefits easier to access; and
WHEREAS Vigilance must be maintained in order to oppose proposals that undermine the effectiveness of
Social Security for low-income older adults, whether through changing how benefits are calculated, raising
the retirement age, or implementing tax cuts that would jeopardize the programs’ overall financial stability;
and
WHEREAS Supplemental Security Income (SSI) is a crucial program for low-income older adults and
people with disabilities who are not able to work enough to make ends meet. However, its outdated rules and
[5]
requirements exclude many of the people it is supposed to help ; and
WHEREAS Regardless of economic status or where we live, we should all be able to live and age in
accessible, affordable, and age-friendly housing in our communities. Yet, older adults are the fastest growing
age group experiencing homelessness. Nationally, almost one in three older renter households pays more than
half of their monthly income in rent, leaving them just one surprise medical bill away from being pushed into
the streets; and
WHEREAS Housing support advocacy should be available to address older adult homelessness so older
adults can have the housing stability they need and a place to receive home care. Reducing federal housing
[6]
programs and supports would harm older adults with the greatest economic needs ; and
WHEREAS All of us are aging, and all of us have a stake in how older adults live and thrive in our families
and communities. The Biden-Harris Administration passed rules that protect older adults from discrimination
and ensure access to services. These crucial rules, such as the Health Care Rights Rule (Sec. 1557), the
Nondiscrimination in Health Care on the Basis of Disability Rule (Sec. 504), the Medicaid Access Rule, and
Nursing Facility Staffing Rules, are under attack through litigation and may be subject to rollbacks; and
WHEREAS historically, programs that rely upon SNAP benefits, Medicare, and Medicaid will be the first to
suffer under federal funding cuts, severely impacting their ability to provide critical services, support, and
resources to seniors and other vulnerable populations who depend on them in Central Harlem and beyond;
and
WHEREAS Seniors are increasingly targeted by fraud, with benefits often stolen through scams and identity
theft. Many rely on the fair hearing process to challenge fraudulent activity and recover stolen benefits, but
proposed staffing and administrative cuts will further delay or prevent access to these essential legal remedies,
leaving seniors without crucial support for extended periods.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Manhattan Community Board 10 strongly urges the protection and
strengthening of essential federal programs, including Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security, and Supplemental
Security Income (SSI)—that are critical to the health, housing, and economic security of older adults in our
community and across the nation, and firmly condemns any efforts to reduce, restrict, or dismantle these life-
sustaining programs;
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Manhattan Community Board 10 calls for increased investment in the
agencies and systems that serve older adults, including adequate staffing, infrastructure, and oversight at the
Social Security Administration, the Department of Health and Human Services, the Department of Veterans
Affairs, and housing support services, to ensure timely and equitable access to care, benefits, and resources;
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Manhattan Community Board 10 calls upon all of our federal elected
officials to actively defend and advance the rights, dignity, and well-being of older adults, and to use every
tool available to prevent any policy changes that would reduce access to healthcare, housing, or income
security for seniors in our community.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Manhattan Community Board 10 urges specific safeguards and
immediate attention to the stability and responsiveness of SNAP, Medicare, and Medicaid-supported
programs, including systems for fraud resolution and benefit recovery, so that seniors are not left without
recourse or support in times of vulnerability.

title: March 31, 2025
resolution_text_full:
March 31, 2025
Max Hollein
Marina Kellen French Director and Chief Executive Officer
The Metropolitan Museum of Art
1000 Fifth Avenue
New York, NY 10028
RE: Community Engagement in Harlem-centric Exhibitions
Dear Mr. Hollein,
I am writing to formally urge The Metropolitan Museum of Art to deepen its engagement with Harlem’s
community boards when curating exhibitions that showcase the culture, history, and artistic contributions
of Harlem’s Black and Latino populations. While the Met has long been recognized as a steward of global
art and history, meaningful representation demands that exhibitions not merely display cultural narratives
but also involve the communities that have lived, shaped, and continue to define those narratives.
Harlem is not just a subject of historical and artistic interest, it is a living, breathing community with deep
cultural legacies and contemporary vibrancy. However, too often, institutions curate exhibitions about
Harlem and its people without engaging those who carry its stories. Community boards, as democratically
elected bodies representing Harlem’s residents, offer an invaluable conduit for ensuring authenticity,
equity, and reciprocity in representation. Their involvement would enhance curatorial efforts, deepen
public engagement, and affirm that Harlem’s culture is not simply an artifact of study but a continuing
legacy.
Beyond courtesy, this is an issue of cultural stewardship and institutional accountability. Representation
in spaces like the Met shapes public perception, historical record, and access to opportunities for Harlem-
based artists, historians, and cultural workers. A failure to include Harlem’s community voices risks
reducing its culture to mere spectacle, rather than honoring it as a lived and evolving identity. The Met
has the power, and the responsibility, to ensure that Harlem’s artistic and cultural contributions are told
with integrity, by and with the very people who have created them.
I encourage the museum to establish a formal collaboration with Harlem’s community boards, ensuring
that exhibitions featuring Black and Latino culture from Harlem are shaped with input from those who
hold these histories in their hands. This could include advisory panels, community partnerships, and
shared decision-making in exhibition planning. Such an approach would set a new precedent for
institutions engaging with historically marginalized communities in ways that are not extractive, but
reciprocal and empowering.
Manhattan Community Board 10 voted unanimously in-support of this letter at the March General Board
Meeting on March 5, 2025 with _31_ votes in support, _0_ Recusals and _0_ Abstentions. We look forward
to your response and the opportunity to discuss how the Met can take meaningful steps toward a more
engaged and representative relationship with Harlem’s communities.
In Solidarity,
Kimberly McLaurin
Marquis A. Harrison Kimberly McLaurin
Board Chairperson Chair, Arts and Culture Committee
Manhattan Community Board 10 Manhattan Community Board 10

title: Resolution To Support the Holcombe Rucker Park Playground Reconstruction
resolution_text_full:
Resolution To Support the Holcombe Rucker Park Playground Reconstruction
WHEREAS Holcombe Rucker Park (Park ID M216) is a 3.05 acre park spanning West 155th
Street and Frederick Douglass Boulevard to the Harlem River Drive in the Borough of
Manhattan in Community Board 10 (CB 10); and
WHEREAS NYC Parks plans to upgrade the Holcombe Rucker Park, while preserving its
renowned character, through architectural technologies and innovative reconstruction; and
WHEREAS the mayoral funded $6.62 million reconstruction is a Community Parks Initiative
(CPI) Project; and
WHEREAS The Holcombe Rucker Park National Commemorative Site Act, signed into law on
January 4th, 2025 by President Joseph R. Biden. The Bill was introduced By Congressman
Adriano Espaillat who guided the legislation successfully through the the U.S. Congress and
U.S. Senate to garner unanimous support in both houses. The Harlem historic park is now
designated as the Holcombe Rucker Park National Commemorative Site; and
WHEREAS In addition to the children’s playground the park houses the Greg Marius basketball
court, a baseball field, handball courts and restroom; and
WHEREAS Following CB 10’s review, this design must be approved by the Public Design
Commission and then go through the procurement process before a contract can be
awarded. Construction may begin in late 2026 or early 2027 and be completed one year later;
and
WHEREAS the goals of the reconstruction include:
• Improved access, circulation and sight lines within the park
• Provision of more fun and play experiences for children of all abilities
• Enhancement and expansion of seating options for people of all ages
• Expanded use of available areas with walking paths within the park with additional green-
space and plantings for aesthetics and stormwater mitigation
• Upgrade and expansion of the spray shower
• Addition of fitness areas and equipment
• Respect for the legacy of Holcombe Rucker; and
WHEREAS The scope of work will include the following features:
• A more Complete playground: The playground has been reorganized to use the space
more efficiently, and maximize the play experiences, sports opportunities and seating,
gathering and picnicking options.
• A more Cohesive playground: Circulation has been thoughtfully designed to provide a
system of wider, noisier primary and narrower, quieter secondary paths, which offer
different types of interactions, and flow seamlessly through the various play, sports, seating
and picnicking areas.
• A more Coherent playground: Drawing on the legendary, world renowned, and nationally
designated commemorative site status of Holcombe Rucker Park as the center of the
basketball universe, where the sport evolved from its local and regional stature to one of
the most internationally loved and revered sport of all time, the design motif throughout the
entire park is basketball, which is evident from afar and in the close-up details, from the
basketball topped entry columns to the dynamic, multidimensional basketball spray shower
to the basketball-like orbs arcing above all the play units and more.
• A central Entrance corridor and bench lined alle create a strong, axial entrance into the
park and leads straight to the central water play feature.
• A huge, central seating and spray circle immersed in multiple and multi-dimensional
basketball inspired features, from the overhead spray pipes shaped like the stitching on a
basketball, the cant of the arced water pipes that evoke a basketball in motion, the
surrounding ring of pavers sized and shaped to resemble a basketball net from above.
• Around the water play is a ring of 16 4-foot benches with companion seating for people in
wheelchairs, And ringing that are a dozen flowering cherry trees to provide shade in this
currently sun-baked central space and powerfully proclaim this spray and seating circle to
be the unmistable heart of the new Holcombe Rucker Park.
• Two quieter bench-lined secondary path branch off from the main entrance alle. Turn to
the right to reach the younger kids play area, and to the left to reach the older kids play and
fitness, adult fitness and the sports courts.
• Accessible 5-12 play unit ramps up to two levels, basketball motif, with high spiral slide,
ladders, bridges, multiple challenge climbers, interactive and sensory play panels.
• Accessible 2-5 play unit, basketball motif, many accessible ground level elements, child-
friendly climbers, low slide, bridge and interactive, visual and sensory play panels, and
opportunities to retreat into more secluded play for children on the spectrum.
• Six 10-foot high swings
• Five 8-foot high swing, one of which is accessible.
• A playfully seal coated run-around grove for older kids with infinite opportunities to create
their own games and paths.
• A "tween" fitness area for the 10-13 year olds who want a higher degree of fitness and
challenge than the 5-12 climbers.
• Adult fitness area for those 13 and over.
• A multi-generational music area sits behind the seating and spray circle and completes the
active uses.
• The path from West 155th to the back entrance at Harlem River Drive has become the
picnic corridor, with five picnic table alcoves.
• The midpoint of the picnic corridor will be sited a new, enlarged public restroom building,
with three toilet/urinal fixtures each for men and women. This Contract will closely follow
the Playground reconstruction, but not sure of exact timing.
• There will be new water service with drinking fountains and bottle filler.
• There will be new storm sewer system with onsite stormwater management practices.
• There will be many more park light poles, which produce pedestrian scale even lighting to
replace the glaring floodlighting.
• The primary path pavement will be decorative and multi-colored concrete pavers similar to
Bennerson Playground.
• Flat topped seating boulders will be scattered through to recall the bedrock outcrops that
are common in this neighborhood.
• Many new plant beds are being added, especially along the two bordering streets to screen
the bleak urban views of the 155th Street viaduct and self-storage warehouse, and of the
overly wide and car-strewn Frederick Douglas Boulevard. We will select plants that not
known to trigger asthma attacks.
WHEREAS The park, which houses the reigning hallowed ground of street-ball courts, is named
after Holcombe Rucker, a local teacher and a playground director for the New York City
Department of Parks and Recreation. Mr. Rucker started a basketball tournament in 1950 in
order to help less fortunate youth stay off the streets and aim for college careers; and
WHEREAS Since 1969, Holcombe Rucker Park has been a source of incalculable pride and
entertainment for Harlemites as well as basketball enthusiasts the world over. What began in
1956 with Holcombe Rucker’s youth tournament, which would lead to 700 Harlem youth
receiving college scholarships, was carried on and expanded with each passing generation.
Bob McCullough continued this legacy with the Rucker Pro Am tournament and Each One
Teach One program, providing young people a source of pride and inspiration over the
decades. Greg Marius would take up the mantle with the Entertainer’s Basketball Classic,
inspiring countless youth from NYC and beyond to achieve greatness. Both of these
tournaments inspired basketball players throughout the world and drew the respect and
participation of some of the world’s greatest athletes and cultural icons; and
WHEREAS Many who played at the iconic park in the Rucker Tournament achieved a level of
fame for their abilities, with several having gone on to play in the National Basketball
Association (NBA); and
WHEREAS Mr. Rucker gave Black players an opportunity to play at a time when the NBA,
founded in 1949, first started. At the time there were only 1 or 2 Blacks per team. There were
few avenues like the Harlem Globe Trotters where teams of Blacks played together. In addition,
players who were not able to go to college had the option to go to the Rucker to play; and
WHEREAS Many professional basketball players have played at the court even after gaining
prominence. Many others developed their basketball skills at Rucker prior to becoming notable
in the sport, including: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Kenny Anderson, Nate Archibald, Metta
Sandiford-Artest, Sylvester Blye, Conney Hawkins, Roger Brown, Julius Erving, Bill Bradley, Joe
Hammond, Earl Manigault, Jackie Jackson, Richard “Pee Wee” Kirkland, Larry “Bone Collector”
Williams, Rafer “Skip to My Lou” Alston, Herman “Helicopter” Knowlings, Conrad “McNasty”
Macrae, Charlie Scott and Wilt Chamberlain; and
WHEREAS The Greg Marius Court was refurbished in 2021 to include: (1) custom-made
basketball goals, styled after the backboards and hoops in the 30 NBA arenas and practice
facilities; making it the only outdoor court in the world with these high-quality goals, (2) a new
surface for the court, eliminating the cracks and other defects in the current pavement, (3) new
bleachers and team benches, (4) new scoreboard, (5) new gates and (6) repairs to the fence;
and
WHEREAS Rucker Park was featured in the TNT film: “On Hallowed Ground: Streetball
Champions of Rucker Park” which aired in 2000 and won a Sports Emmy Award,The Real:
Rucker Park Legends---True Harlem Story (2006), #Rucker50 Documentary (2016), Undefeated
The Roger Brown Story - PBS (2013), It was also featured in the 2018 film: “Uncle Drew”; and
Above The Rim (1994); and
WHEREAS The design provides an opportunity to honor Holcombe Rucker at the main entrance
to the playground on Frederick Douglass Boulevard, where two attractive pillars will have
decorative features in the form of basketballs on top. Space would be available on the front of
the pillars facing the street for bronze plaques; one could have a bas-relief portrait of Rucker,
and the other could be inscribed with a short biography; and
WHEREAS The legendary basketball players who played over the years on what is now known
as the Greg Marius Court also could be honored with plaques on the numerous benches on the
paths throughout the redesigned playground. These plaques could have the names of players
who are still living which would not be possible with a permanent artwork such as a “Walk of
Fame” in the park. NYC Parks Department will be working with the Holcombe Rucker memorial
committee to identify possible locations where a statue of Holcombe Rucker could be placed in
the playground and possible alternatives to the proposed “Walk of Fame.” All of these memorial
ideas would require some degree of community fundraising since the policy is to have statues,
plaques and similar items in parks paid for with private funds and for statues in particular to
have maintenance endowments; and
WHEREAS Community Board 10 calls upon NYC Parks to maintain the 7-foot-high fencing
along Frederick Douglass Boulevard and not to lower it to 4 feet in the interest of public safety,
especially when large crowds are attempting to attend basketball games at the court adjacent to
the playground; and
WHEREAS a Coalition of the Holcombe Rucker Family, The Greg Marius Family, Each One
Teach One and HCCI presented at the November 8th, 2024 Manhattan Community Board 10
Parks and Recreation Committee meeting to introduce a proposal to capture the essence of the
Rucker Park story in a compelling visual format, around the park itself, for local residents,
players and visiting fans to enjoy. The goal is to enshrine the historic legacy of the Rucker Park;
its community power and transformation, while telling the story of the historical figures for
generations to come; and
WHEREAS NYC Parks held a Holcombe Rucker Playground Reconstruction Community Input
Meeting via Zoom on June 27th, 2024; and
WHEREAS NYC Parks and Recreation architects presented design plans to the Parks and
Recreation Committee on February 26th, 2025, where the Committee had quorum and voted
unanimously to support the project; and
WHEREAS The Parks and Recreation Committee presented to the Executive Committee on
February 12th, 2025, where the Committee had quorum and voted 6 yes, 0 opposed, 0
abstentions and 0 recusals to support the project; and
WHEREAS the Parks and Recreation Committee presented to the Manhattan CB10’s Full
Board on March 5th, 2025, which had quorum and voted unanimously in-support of the park
reconstruction ; and
THEREFORE NOW be it resolved that Manhattan Community Board 10 supports the
Community Parks Initiative design plans to upgrade the Holcombe Rucker Park, while
preserving its renowned character, through architectural technologies and innovative
reconstruction of the Holcombe Rucker Park playground.

title: March 6, 2025
resolution_text_full:
March 6, 2025
Sue Donoghue
Commissioner
New York City Department of Parks & Recreation
830 Fifth Ave
New York, NY 10065
Re: West Harlem Art Fund Harlem Sculpture Garden in Jackie Robinson Park
Dear Commissioner Donoghue,
Manhattan Community Board 10 is writing this letter to recommend the West Harlem Art Fund
Sculpture Garden installation in Jackie Robinson Park. The proposed art exhibition is
scheduled for May 2nd, 2025 and will run through October 30th, 2025.
The West Harlem Art Fund (WHAF) is a twenty-seven year old, public art and new media
organization. WHAF seeks opportunities for artists and creative professionals throughout NYC
and beyond wishing to showcase and share their talent. The West Harlem Art Fund presents art
and culture in open and public spaces to add aesthetic interest; promote historical and cultural
heritage; and support community involvement in local development.
The following art pieces and corresponding artists are proposed for showcasing at Jackie Robinson
Park:
• “Bound Medium” - Dianne Smith
• “Skate Boarding Cat” - Eunkyung Lee
• “Painted Welded Steel” - Carole Eisner Chiara
• “The Tower” - Margaret Roleke
• “Spout” - Luke Schumacher
• “Harlequin” - Michael Poast
• “Land Art” - Laurie Sheridan
• “Tree Sits On Bench At Park With Books” - An Pham
The selections will be anchored as needed and positioned at various locations between 145th and
150th Streets. (Please see attached presentation).
Ms. Savona Bailey McClain is the Executive Director & Chief Curator for The West Harlem Art
Fund, Inc. a twenty-three year old public art organization and curatorial collective serving
neighborhoods around the City. Her public art installations have been seen in the New York Times,
Art Daily, Artnet, Los Angeles Times, Huffington Post among others. McClain has installed works
in Times Square, DUMBO, Soho, Governors Island and Harlem. Noted works include The H in
Harlem, Counting Sheep, Story Piles, East River Flows and Loosely Coupled. Ms. McClain is a
registered local historian with the Office of the Manhattan Borough President, a member of Art
Table and radio podcast host for State of the Arts NYC heard on several audio platforms.
Ms. Savona Bailey McClain presented to the Parks and Recreation Committee on February 12th,
2025. The Jackie Robinson Park Conservancy is in support of the project. This project proposed
for Jackie Robinson Park which is one of the four Harlem Historic Parks will be the second year

title: March 6, 2025
resolution_text_full:
March 6, 2025
Sue Donoghue
Commissioner
New York City Department of Parks & Recreation
830 Fifth Ave
New York, NY 10065
Re: Augusta Savage Commemoration By Monumental Women
Dear Commissioner Donoghue,
Community Board 10 is writing this letter in support of Monumental Women’s Initiative to
commemorate Augusta Savage through a work of public art. We are hopeful this tribute will be
in one of the CB 10 parks. It is particularly fitting to honor Ms. Savage at a site within the borders
of CB 10, where she lived and worked.
Augusta Savage (born Augusta Christine Fells; February 29, 1892 – March 27, 1962) was an
American sculptor associated with the Harlem Renaissance. She was also a teacher whose studio
was important to the careers of a generation of African American artists who would become
nationally known. She worked for equal rights for African Americans in the arts. As the creator
of busts of prominent African Americans such as W.E.B. Du Bois and James Weldon Johnson,
Savage also focused on representing everyday people from Harlem (e.g. “Gamin”, untitled “Girl
With Pigtails”). Her monumental plaster sculpture “Lift Every Voice and Sing” (renamed “The
Harp” by others), created for the 1939 World’s Fair held in Queens, New York was viewed and
admired by more than 5 million fair attendees. Ms. Savage endured the travesty of having her
masterpiece demolished after the World’s Fair end because she had no money to store it or have it
cast in bronze.
Ms. Savage was an important part of the Harlem Renaissance and one of America’s foremost
African American women artists. She worked as a sculptor and educator and fought against sexism
and racism. Eighty–five years after its debut, Savage’s pivotal and inspiring story and artwork
deserves to be known by a new generation.
In honor of Black History Month 2024 and the leap year February 29th birthday of Augusta
Savage, Monumental Women announced the formation of a coalition to honor Ms. Savage’s
achievements in art, her opposition to sexism and racism in the arts and her commitment to
educating the next generation of African American artists.
Monumental Women, a 501c(3) all-volunteer nonprofit was created in 2014 with the initial goal
of breaking the bronze ceiling and creating the first statue of real women in Central Park’s 167-
year history. The Central Park monument of Women’s Rights Pioneers Sojourner Truth, Susan B.
Anthony, and Elizabeth Cady Stanton was unveiled on August 26th, 2020, the centennial
anniversary of the ratification and certification of the 19th “Votes For Women” amendment to the
constitution. Monumental Women’s experience with carrying through the complicated process of
forming partnerships, raising substantial funds (almost entirely private), conducting a design
competition, gathering the many necessary community endorsements and city permits - all while
meeting their timeline in the midst of a pandemic (2020) — demonstrates they are capable of
successfully managing the many challenges of creating a piece of beautiful and inspiring public
art in New York City. The project timeline is proposed for 2025-2028.
Monumental Women presented the proposed project at the Manhattan Community Board 10
Parks and Recreation Committee on February 12th, 2025.
Manhattan CB10 finds Monumental Women’s Augusta Savage Initiative collaborative project,
which will honor and encapsulate the profound and historic legacy of Augusta Savage to be of
phenomenal merit. On March 5, 2025, Manhattan Community Board 10’s General Board
convened on March 5, 2025 and unanimously voted in-support of the project.

title: March 14, 2025
resolution_text_full:
March 14, 2025
The Honorable Charles E. Schumer
The Honorable Kirsten Gillibrand
United States Senate
Washington DC 20510
Dear Senator Schumer and Senator Gillibrand,
I write today to express support for the FY 2026 Congressionally Directed Spending Request (CDSR) submitted by
CUNY SPH. With this funding, CUNY SPH will create a new Public Health Emergency Preparedness and Response
Training Hub (PHEPR-TH).
As of 2023, the U.S. public health workforce needed 80,000 additional full-time workers in state and local settings,
primarily in health departments, to provide core services. An additional loss of 129,000 workers is projected by this
year, with updated data expected in summer 2025. Even more public health workers, who are typically not counted
in official reports, are needed in non-governmental organizations. In New York State alone, a 2022 workforce study
by the New York State Association of County Health Officials (NYSACHO) revealed a 26% decline in full-time
local health department (LHD) employees since 2019, with temporary federal and state emergency funding creating
an unstable influx of short-term staff for COVID-19 response efforts. As these employees are not permanent and
leave when funding runs out, LHDs will face a significant loss of staff and experience, even as they continue to
manage current, emergent, and unforeseen public health threats. More than ever, this entire workforce needs training
in public health and healthcare emergency response and preparedness.
CUNY SPH’s PHEPR-TH is uniquely positioned to meet demand in the current and future public health workforce.
PHEPR-TH will be available to graduate students, public health and safety professionals, and community members
who wish to develop or strengthen their skills and credentials for career advancement to address future emergencies
with a sound scientific basis. The PHEPR-TH will establish a new certificate program in Public Health Emergency
Preparedness and Response at CUNY SPH that can serve the growing need for training in PHEPR among the public
health and healthcare workforce that is unique in its curriculum and community connections. The PHEPR-TH will
expand CUNY SPH program offerings, attract new students to public health, further career and professional training
for graduate students and professionals, and fill a major gap in the public health and healthcare workforce.
Moreover, given CUNY SPH’s strong online curriculum, this training will be accessible locally, nationally, and
internationally, broadening its reach. Federal funding is vital for CUNY SPH to launch the training hub, and will
support your constituents with:
• Increased access to knowledge and skills that are in-demand from employers
• Training to fill current and future positions paying living wages in the public health workforce
• Increased ability to serve their community and protect its well-being in times of acute need
Manhattan Community Board 10 voted unanimously to support the creation of a hub by the CUNY School for
Public Health during the March General Board Meeting on March 5, 2025. We are confident that communities,
particularly in Harlem and many others, will benefit from the increased workforce training PHEPR-TH will provide,
both as participants and as recipients of the services those trained can offer. I encourage you to move this proposal
forward to the Appropriations Committee and vigorously support it throughout the process.

title: March 14, 2025
resolution_text_full:

Dear Senator Schumer and Senator Gillibrand,
I write today to express support for the FY 2026 Congressionally Directed Spending Request (CDSR)
submitted by CUNY SPH Center for Innovation in Mental Health (CUNY CIMH). With this funding,
CUNY CIMH will develop and implement a Community Care Model for Mental Health Wellness.
There is an urgent need to expand access to mental health services, especially in historically underserved
communities where the traditional healthcare infrastructure has often been insufficient. This proposal is a
timely and necessary response to the growing mental health crisis, exacerbated by the COVID-19 pandemic
and systemic inequities. It has the potential to transform mental health access and strengthen community
resilience in New York City and beyond.
CUNY CIMH has consistently demonstrated expertise in mental health task-sharing, an evidence-based
approach that empowers non-clinical professionals—such as community leaders, educators, and peer
support specialists—to deliver essential services. Their successful programs, including Harlem Strong,
Building Resilience in Youth, and Jobs Plus, highlight their ability to expand access to mental healthcare,
improve service quality, and strengthen community resilience.
The Community Care Model for Mental Health Wellness will build on these successes by refining task-
sharing to meet the unique needs of diverse communities. This initiative will address critical gaps in mental
health care, especially in underserved communities, by leveraging community networks to integrate mental
health and wellness support into neighborhoods. It will include scalable training materials to help
communities identify mental health concerns, provide timely interventions, and connect individuals to
resources. This initiative will increase access to care, reduce stigma, and foster a culture of trust and support
while building resilience in vulnerable populations.
During the March General Board Meeting on March 5, 2025, Manhattan Community Board 10 voted
unanimously in support of the CUNY School of Public Health’s efforts to develop a Community Care
Model for Mental Health Wellness. I am confident that our communities, and many others, will benefit from
this expansion of the mental health task-sharing approach, bringing critical services to underserved areas
while increasing the size and availability of the mental health workforce. I encourage you to move this
proposal forward to the Appropriations Committee and vigorously support it throughout the process.

title: April 8, 2025
resolution_text_full:
April 8, 2025
Louis A. Molina
Commissioner

Dear Commissioner Molina and Acting Commissioner Morse,
On behalf of the Manhattan Community Board 10, I write to express our strong support for naming
the new Public Health Lab at 137th Street in Harlem in honor of the late Dr. Hazel N. Dukes. This
facility presents a unique opportunity to enhance public health resources in our community and to
pay tribute to a visionary leader whose life’s work was dedicated to advancing civil rights, social
justice, and health equity.
Dr. Dukes was a pillar of our community and a guiding force in the fight for justice and healthcare
accessibility. Her legacy is deeply interwoven with the history of iconic civil rights leaders such
as Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Malcolm X, and Congressman Adam Clayton Powell Jr. These
historic figures inspired and reinforced her steadfast commitment to ensuring justice, equality, and
healthcare access for all. As an advocate and mentor, Dr. Dukes uplifted generations of leaders,
ensuring that the movement for civil rights and social justice continues in strong and capable hands.
Dr. Dukes’ profound impact on public health was evident through her service as the Chairperson
of the Health and Human Services Committee of Community Board 10. In this role, she led
discussions and convened meetings that facilitated essential conversations regarding the
development of this very project, the new Public Health Lab in Harlem. Her leadership in shaping
discourse around public health initiatives makes the naming of this facility in her honor an
especially fitting tribute to her enduring contributions.
Beyond her work with Community Board 10, Dr. Dukes served as the President of the New York
State Conference of the NAACP, where she relentlessly advocated for the rights of marginalized
communities and sought to dismantle systemic barriers to healthcare. Her collaboration with the
New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, public health campaigns, the American
Cancer Society, state and federal agencies was instrumental in advancing policies, programs, and
public campaigns that improved health outcomes for Harlem and beyond. One example of her
impact was her recent involvement, prior to her passing, in the public campaign to end the sale of
menthol cigarettes to reduce health disparities.
While we understand that a formal naming process for the Public Health Lab may not yet be in
place, we strongly urge you, Acting Commissioner Morse, to champion and expedite the
establishment of such a process to properly recognize Dr. Dukes’ extraordinary contributions. Her
tireless dedication to public health and social justice has left an indelible mark on our city, and
naming this lab in her honor would enshrine her legacy for future generations.
Dr. Dukes’ lifelong work has been widely recognized with numerous accolades, including the
Candace Award for Community Service from the National Coalition of 100 Black Women, the
Economic and Business Award from the Women’s Black Agenda, the NAACP’s Spingarn Medal,
and the historic distinction of being the first civilian to administer the oath of office to New York
State Governor Kathy Hochul. These honors reflect her unwavering commitment to advocating
for social justice and health equity.
As we continue the work she so passionately led, we believe that naming the new Public Health
Lab after Dr. Hazel N. Dukes would serve as a profound reminder of her lasting impact on our
community and as an inspiration for generations to come. The members of Manhattan Community
Board 10, along with a broad coalition of community leaders and organizations, stand united in
supporting this initiative.
Thank you for your time and consideration. Manhattan Community Board 10 voted unanimously
in-support of this letter at the April General Board Meeting on Wednesday, April 2, 2025 with
34 Yes, 0 Recusals, and 0 Abstentions. We look forward to your support in ensuring that Dr.
Hazel N. Dukes’ legacy is honored in a manner befitting her unparalleled contributions to public
health and civil rights.

title: Resolution Condemning Efforts to Dismantle the U.S. Department of Education
resolution_text_full:
Resolution Condemning Efforts to Dismantle the U.S. Department of Education
WHEREAS, on March 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order titled
"Improving Educational Outcomes by Empowering Parents, States, and Communities," which
seeks to dismantle the U.S. Department of Education (ED) and transfer all authority over education
to the states.
WHEREAS, the U.S. Department of Education, established in 1980, has been instrumental in
promoting educational excellence and ensuring equal access to education across the nation. Its
responsibilities include administering federal funding to states and school districts, enforcing civil
rights protections, and conducting research on educational institutions.
WHEREAS, the ED plays a pivotal role in managing federal student aid programs, including Pell
Grants and federal student loans, which have enabled countless students from low-income families
to pursue higher education and improve their socioeconomic status.
WHEREAS, in the 2023-24 academic year, over 6.2 million students nationwide relied on Pell
Grants to afford higher education, with thousands of students from Community Board 10’s district
benefiting from these grants to attend colleges and universities. The dismantling of the ED would
put these crucial financial aid programs at risk, potentially denying many students the opportunity
to pursue post-secondary education and limiting their ability to achieve economic mobility.
WHEREAS, the loss of federal student aid oversight would increase the risk of predatory lending
practices by private loan providers, disproportionately harming first-generation college students,
low-income students, and students of color.
WHEREAS, the ED oversees critical programs such as Title I funding for disadvantaged schools,
the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) for students with disabilities, and the
National School Lunch Program, which provides free and reduced-price meals to eligible students.
WHEREAS, New York City Public Schools serve approximately 912,064 students, with 16.3%
identified as English Language Learners and 23% as students with disabilities. The ED's support
is vital in addressing the diverse needs of these students.
WHEREAS, Community Board 10 encompasses Central Harlem, which includes NYC
Geographic Districts 3 and 5. District 3 serves approximately 19,374 students across 43 public
schools, while District 5 serves approximately 20,000 students across 35 public schools.
WHEREAS, within District 3, approximately 58% of students are eligible for free or reduced-
price lunch, 24% are students with disabilities, and 13% are English Language Learners. In District
5, nearly 73% of students qualify for free or reduced-price lunch, 25% are students with
disabilities, and 14% are English Language Learners. These numbers underscore the essential role
of federal funding in supporting students who rely on these services for academic success and well-
being.
WHEREAS, federal funding through the ED supports various programs within Districts 3 and 5,
including initiatives for English Language Learners, students with disabilities, and economically
disadvantaged students. These programs are essential in providing equitable educational
opportunities and resources.
WHEREAS, there are ongoing efforts in various states to undermine comprehensive education by
promoting curricula that emphasize only the positive aspects of American history while neglecting
significant portions of our collective past. Federal oversight has historically been crucial in
enforcing civil rights and advancing educational equity.
WHEREAS, the potential dismantling of the ED threatens the continuation and effectiveness of
these programs, jeopardizing the educational outcomes and well-being of students in our
community.
WHEREAS, constitutionally, the President of the United States does not have the unilateral
authority to eliminate a federal department such as the ED, as such an action requires congressional
approval. The attempt to bypass this legislative process raises significant concerns about the
overreach of executive power.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Manhattan Community Board 10 strongly condemns
any efforts to dismantle the U.S. Department of Education, recognizing such actions as detrimental
to the students and families within our district and across the nation.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Manhattan Community Board 10 urges Federal, State, and
City Representatives to oppose any initiatives aimed at weakening or eliminating the ED,
emphasizing the importance of sustained Federal support for education.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Manhattan Community Board 10 affirms the importance
of Federal financial aid programs in making higher education accessible to all students, particularly
those from marginalized communities, and opposes any efforts that would weaken these resources.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Manhattan Community Board 10 commits to ongoing
efforts to educate and inform the public about their rights and the implications of dismantling the
ED, ensuring that residents remain engaged in advocating for equitable and well-funded public
education;
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that the Chairperson of Manhattan Community Board 10 is
empowered to establish relationships, sign letters, petitions, and utilize other tools to ensure that
Community Board 10 actively opposes efforts that undermine our education system and harm our
students; Manhattan Community Board 10’s full board voted unanimously to approved this
resolution at the April General Board Meeting on Wednesday, April 2, 2025 with 34 Yes, 0
Recusals, and 0 Abstentions.

One45 For Harlem Resolution
Manhattan Community Board 10
RESOLUTION: To disapprove with conditions the private application by One45 Lenox LLC for a
zoning map amendment, a zoning text amendment to modify Appendix F, two zoning special permits (ZS)
to change height and setback regulations, and a zoning certification (ZC) to allow additional curb cuts to
facilitate the development of a 34-story mixed use complex with approximately 968 units of which 291
units will be permanently affordable. The development will be located at 685-691 Lenox Avenue and 112-
150 West 145th Street in Manhattan Community District 10.
WHEREAS, One45 Lenox LLC development group is seeking approval of a Uniform Land Use Review
Process (hereafter known as "ULURP") application for C250115ZMM, N250116ZRM, C250117ZSM,
C250118ZSM, and N250119ZCM for a zoning map amendment to rezone the area from a C8-3 and R7-
2/C1-4 to a C4-6, a zoning text amendment to modify Appendix F in order to designate the development
site in the Mandated Inclusionary Housing (MIH) program, two zoning special permits, and a CPC zoning
certification to allow additional curb cuts; and
WHEREAS, the C250115ZMM application is seeking approval for a zoning map amendment to rezone
the area from a C8-3 and R7-2/C1-4 to a C4-6 zone with 10.83 residential floor area, and maximum
commercial FAR of 3.4; and
WHEREAS, the N2501116ZRM application seeks approval for a zoning text amendment to Appendix F
of the Zoning Resolution mapping a Mandatory Inclusionary Housing (“MIH”) area Option 2, by proposing
that 30% (291 apartments) of the units will be permanently affordable with an average 80% of AMI (area
median income); and
WHEREAS, the C250117ZSM application seeks a special permit pursuant to Section 74-743 to modify
the height and setback regulations for the banquet hall located on the top floor of Building A, and a
C250118ZSM application seeking a special permit to waive residential parking regulations is terminated
due to the recently approval of the City of Yes for Housing Opportunity eliminating parking requirements
in Manhattan Community Board 10; and
WHEREAS, the N250119ZCM applications seeks a CPC certification to add additional curb cuts: and
WHEREAS, the development site will consist of three buildings, two residential buildings and one
commercial building. Building A will have 537 dwelling units, 12,482 sf of retail space, a 37,766 sf
banquet hall/meeting space located on the top floor, and 40 below-grade accessory residential parking
spaces. Building B will have 431 dwelling units, 14,984 sf of retail space, and 6,563 sf of community
facility space. Building C would provide 8,540 sf of retail space. As previously stated the project would
be located at 685-691 Lenox Avenue and 112-150 West 145th Street in Manhattan Community District 10;
and
WHEREAS, the project will include 968 residential units of which 291 will be designated permanently
affordable. This is an increase of 138 units due the removal of the Museum of Civil Rights from the current
proposal. Of the 291 units, 29 units will be studios, 131 are one-bedrooms, 61 are two-bedrooms, and 20
are three-bedrooms - representing a slight increase from the project previously proposed wherein the total
number of two and three bedroom units was 60; and
WHEREAS, the permanently affordable units will be at AMI levels ranging from 40% to 120% with an
average of 80 %. The community remains concerned that existing AMI levels do not adequately reflect the
needs of community residents including single occupancy middle class households that are excluded from
the income bands proposed, leaving them with only market rate residential options; and
WHEREAS, the One45 Lenox LLC development group also presented an uncertified Enhanced
Affordability Plan that highlighted their partnership with Concern Housing and West Harlem Group
Assistance Inc. to develop 591 affordable units of the total 968 dwelling units. The enhanced affordability
plan included the following:

2. Building A will have 160 affordable units;
3. 130 units of supportive housing with no income requirement;

Inc. The building will include on-site amenities such as a fitness center, library, computer room,
laundry facility, multiple community meeting spaces, outdoor spaces, and free Wi-Fi throughout

7. Staffing would include a Director, Supervisor, Case Managers, Counselors, Property Management
& Maintenance Staff. Program staff would primarily focus on supportive housing residents but
would be available to assist all residents. Priority will be given to hire local and minority candidates
for operational positions.
WHEREAS, One45 Lenox LLC development group presented a draft community benefits agreement

Development and Training division of the New York State Research and Development Authority

underrepresented by minorities and low-income citizens – our goal is to help change that in Harlem.

Brigadier General Charles Young Playground.

emissions in the community
WHEREAS, New York City recently approved the CITY OF YES FOR HOUSING OPPORTUNITY with

at the same AMI levels proposed in this project in Manhattan Community Board 10; and

units especially affordable housing units, we recognize that the district has a limited number of vacant

greater density must be considered; and
WHEREAS, Manhattan Community Board 10 has 60 days to review the One45 for Harlem ULURP
application and render an opinion, which such time to review began on December 11, 2024; and
WHEREAS, Manhattan Community Board 10 facilitated two public hearings on 12/19/24 and 1/16/25
wherein the One45 Lenox LLC development group conducted presentations, received comments from the

responses to questions. Manhattan Community Board 10 also facilitated a community forum on 1/25/25 to
afford the community a final opportunity to provide feedback; and
WHEREAS, Manhattan Community Board 10 members and the community had the following concerns:
a. Central Harlem needs new affordable housing units.
b. Affordable Units/Affordability – 291 permanently affordable units is not sufficient to meet the
needs of the community. The certified project would add 677 market rate units to the community.
Some residents supported the uncertified enhanced affordability plan.
c. According to the 2024 NYU Furman Center, the median household income in Central Harlem in
2022 was $52,000 compared to a citywide median household income of $78,000.
d. The AMI levels outlined for the permanently affordable units are based on income levels that are
too high for Harlem residents and not a true reflection of the actual income of residents of our
District as opposed to an income average of persons outside of the District.
e. Increased Density/Transportation Concerns – Building A and Building B will be 34 stories each,
taller than any building in the surrounding area. Based on the number of residential units (968), it
is estimated that 2000 to 3000 new residents will be added to this area. This increased density will
impact the existing public transportation systems in the area.
f. The IRT#3 train station at 145th Street and Malcom X. Blvd. is a short station that only affords five
subway cars to open on the platforms on Northbound and Southbound trains.. The existing
transportation hubs are not equipped to support the increased density. This can result in an increase
in traffic caused by taxis, rideshare companies, and personal-use vehicles.
g. Contextual Inconsistencies with surrounding community
h. Environmental - part of the development site is a brownfield and dangerously close to an
established flood zone.
i. Displacement - Project will result in the further displacement of Harlem residents who can no
longer afford to live in the community and accelerate the gentrification of the community.
j. Community Benefits presented do not adequately meet the needs of the community, fail to
concretely outline measurable, targeted goals, and do not include formal plans for oversight and
methods of accountability that are legally binding and enforceable.
k. The site is in poor condition and requires revitalization.
WHEREAS, on January 29, 2025, The Executive Committee voted _16 Yes, 7 No, 1 Abstention, and
_1 Recusal to approve the application with conditions.
WHEREAS, on February 5, 2025, at the General Board Meeting, the Board did not approve the
recommendations of the Executive Committee, with 17 Yes, 17 No, 1 Abstention, and 1 Recusal.
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED; Manhattan Community Board 10 DISAPPROVED with
CONDITIONS C250119ZMM, N250116ZRM, C250117ZSM, C250118ZSM, and N250119ZCM
applications for zoning map and zoning text amendments, special permits, and CPC certifications to
facilitate the mixed-use development known as One45 for Harlem during the February 5, 2025 General
Board Meeting, the board voted _19 Yes, 10 No, _5 Abstention, and 1 Recusal.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED; Manhattan Community Board 10 disapproves the application with the
following conditions:
a. Whereas One45 Lenox LLC is proposing a height of 407 ft for Building A and B, CB 10 strongly
recommends a height of 380 ft as the proposed height significantly exceeds the height of any
development in the surrounding area and will create shadows and interfere with sunlight.
b. Whereas One45 Lenox LLC is proposing a community space with approximately 6,550 sf that is
insufficient for a development of this scale. CB 10 strongly recommends an increase to 15,000 sf
in order to create a diverse space of community-based organizations and non-profit providers that
would deliver comprehensive supports and services to the youth in Central Harlem
c. Central Harlem has a moderate risk of flooding. The One45 for Harlem development site is just
outside of the floodplain. CB 10 strongly recommends the implementation of dry and wet
floodproofing of mechanical systems and living spaces consistent with NYC’s Zoning for Coastal
Flood Resiliency in order to mitigate future flooding in the area.
d. Whereas One45 Lenox LLC is proposing 40 below grade parking spaces in Building A, they did
not provide any definitive explanation regarding the assignment of these parking spaces. CB 10
strongly recommends that the development team outline use and designation of parking spaces.
e. All permanently affordable units should be equally distributed throughout both buildings to ensure
equity in design, and to prevent stigma and bias.
f. All tenants should have the same access to all building amenities.
g. The development of a comprehensive, legally binding and enforceable Community Benefits
Agreement.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED; Manhattan Community Board 10 recommends the following:
a. Securing pro-bono legal representation to work with community board, Harlem residents, and local
organizations to create a legally binding and enforceable community benefits agreement.
b. One45 Lenox LLC to create a fund to financially support the various elements to be outlined in the
community benefits agreement that will be created with the community board, community
stakeholders, and elected officials. A percentage of revenue from the banquet hall should be used
to fund aspects of the Community Benefits Agreement.
c. Including more specific, measurable targets and goals and timeline for results in the community
benefits agreement.
d. Increase the amount of community space to 15,000 sf in order to support comprehensive
programming for youth and their families. Reduce the amount of retail space throughout the
development site in order to increase the amount of community space
e. Outline measurable, targeted goals for the youth internship and mentorship initiative that includes
the number of youth to be served, the length of the program, the scope of services, and the list of
committed partners.
f. Community benefits should include technology that brings economic opportunities, education,
healthcare, digital inclusion, civic engagement, and empowerment to the community.
g. Increase the percentage of local hiring from 10% to 50%. While Positive Workforce will train
some residents on various jobs, One45 Lenox LLC should engage other companies with a
successful track record of hiring local residents.
h. Hire a MWBE for construction and a Harlem based business to market and manage One45 for
Harlem.
i. Outline the brownfield remediation efforts for the site and return to the community board to provide
periodic updates.
j. One45 Lenox LLC to acknowledge that the creation, operation and maintenance of a truck stop
along the West 145th Street corridor has had a negative impact on the members of that community
suffering from respiratory illnesses such as Asthma, and to create a fund to support the study and
remediation of the same.
k. Outline plans to mitigate the environmental impacts during the construction phase such as increased
dust, noise, and traffic congestion.
l. Include green spaces and/or environmental amenities which are critical to community health
especially in light of historic health disparities and injustices.
m. Although the development is just outside of the floodplain, the development site should include all
wet and dry floodproofing options identified in NYC’s Zoning for Coastal Flood Resiliency as
Central Harlem has a moderate risk for flooding in this area.
n. Representatives of One45 Lenox LLC will return to the Land Use Committee throughout the
project to provide quarterly updates on the progress and how the developer is tracking against
benchmarks for housing units, rents/affordability, and metrics outlined in the Community Benefits
Agreement.
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, if funding is secured from NYC and/or any other government program
to develop the enhanced affordability plan, Manhattan Community Board 10 demands the following:
1. Concern Housing and West Harlem Group Assistance, Inc. should return to the Manhattan
Community Board 10 to review development plans and solicit further input from the community
as to its supportive and affordable housing needs and the overall planned project during its further
planning stages and once funded and/or approved.
2. At least one representative from both Concern Housing and West Harlem Group Assistance, Inc.
will serve as a member of the One45 Community Advisory Partners.
3. Concern Housing and West Harlem Group Assistance, Inc. will adhere to the same Hire Harlem
parameters as One45 Lenox LLC (at minimum 10% and ideally 50% of those involved in the
construction and ongoing operation of the project will come from Harlem).
4. Concern Housing and West Harlem Group Assistance, Inc. should outline the location of the
amenities previously mentioned in the development and provide clarity regarding use of the
Community Center.
5. One45 Lenox LLC, Concern Housing and West Harlem Group Assistance, Inc. will ensure that
supportive and affordable units are distributed throughout both buildings in the development.
6. Outline plans to mitigate the environmental impacts during the construction phase such as increased
dust, noise, and traffic congestion.
7. Concern Housing and West Harlem Group Assistance, Inc. will maintain communication with the
community board throughout the development of the project to ensure that proposed elements of
the project are completed.
8. Establish an independent oversight committee composed of the community board, Harlem
residents, local organizations, and elected officials to monitor and evaluate commitments made
under the CBA.

title: Resolution Condemning Federal Law Enforcement Immigration Raids and Affirming
resolution_text_full:
Resolution Condemning Federal Law Enforcement Immigration Raids and Affirming
Support for Immigrant Communities
WHEREAS, the United States has a long history of being a beacon for immigrants seeking safety,
opportunity, and freedom, and this diversity has been an essential component of the nation’s
identity and strength; and
WHEREAS, Harlem has historically served as a sanctuary for diverse communities, including
African Americans during the Great Migration, immigrants from the Caribbean, Latin America,
and Africa, and others who sought refuge and opportunity in its vibrant and welcoming
neighborhoods; and
WHEREAS, Manhattan Community Board 10 recognizes the historical injustices perpetrated
against Indigenous peoples, including the theft of their lands, and acknowledges that no human
being is "illegal" on stolen land; and
WHEREAS, policies and measures such as Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and
other Federal Law Enforcement raids instill fear and uncertainty within immigrant communities,
undermining public safety, trust, and the cohesive social fabric that binds our diverse communities
together; and
WHEREAS, the current Federal raids authorized by the President of the United States further
perpetuate a culture of fear, discrimination, and marginalization among immigrant communities,
particularly targeting communities of color; and
WHEREAS, Manhattan Community Board 10 recognizes that creating an environment of
inclusion, understanding, and protection is fundamental to the wellbeing of Harlem’s residents and
its continued role as a cultural and historical hub for people of all backgrounds; and
WHEREAS, the right to legal representation, due process, and humane treatment are enshrined in
the principles of justice that this nation upholds; and
WHEREAS, Manhattan Community Board 10 acknowledges its role as a voice for the community
in advocating for policies and practices that protect and empower all residents, regardless of
immigration status;
THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED, that Manhattan Community Board 10 condemns the
Immigrant raids that are being carried out by Federal Law Enforcement launched by the President
of the United States and any measures that perpetuate a culture of fear, marginalization, and
injustice within immigrant communities; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Manhattan Community Board 10 will work in collaboration
with coalitions and organizations advocating for immigrant rights to ensure that members of our
community are informed and educated about their legal rights; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Manhattan Community Board 10 stands united with the
Harlem community to protect and uplift all its residents, fostering a spirit of inclusion, solidarity,
and justice; and
BE IT FURTHER RESOLVED, that Manhattan Community Board 10 reaffirms Harlem’s legacy
as a diverse and inclusive sanctuary for all and will continue to support measures that uphold the
dignity, rights, and humanity of every individual in our community.
Manhattan Community Board 10 voted unanimously in-support of this resolution during the
February General Board on February 5, 2025 with 36 Yes, 0 No , 0 Recusals 0 Abstentions
